questions.prompt: What is the core move in the strategy of the void?
choices: Deny the opponent a clean target by distributing exposure
Disappear completely from every conflict
Publicly threaten retaliation before any attack lands

explanation.gentle: The chapter defines the void as denied target rather than magical invisibility.
explanation.direct: Start with the target logic: the structure changes attack efficiency by removing one decisive strike point.
explanation.competitive: The point is to make one blow worth less, not to float into mist.

questions.prompt: Why are fixed centers dangerous for weaker operators?
choices: They make morale permanently stronger
They give the opponent a clear node to isolate and hit
They prevent observers from understanding the conflict

explanation.gentle: Fixed centers simplify the attacker's job because one hit can be made to look decisive.
explanation.direct: Look at the geometry: a visible hub turns strategy into targeting aid for the stronger side.
explanation.competitive: One legible node is an invitation to a kill shot.

questions.prompt: What is the main reversal built into this chapter?
choices: Any decentralized team automatically becomes more accountable
The strategy only works in private conflicts
Too much diffusion can preserve survival while destroying action clarity

explanation.gentle: The warning is that resilience can flip into drift if ownership disappears.
explanation.direct: Notice the reversal: diffusion stops helping when your own side can no longer decide or move clearly.
explanation.competitive: A system can dodge the enemy and still lose to its own fog.

questions.prompt: Odalys is being pushed to appoint one permanent spokesperson because it would look cleaner. What best fits the chapter?
choices: Keep public burden distributed while preserving internal decision clarity
Accept one face because observers always reward simplicity
Stop communicating with allies so the rival learns nothing

explanation.gentle: Odalys gains by removing the obvious person a stronger rival wants to isolate.
explanation.direct: Focus on the strike path: one permanent face creates the clean target the strategy is trying to deny.
explanation.competitive: Do not volunteer one throat to grab when shared exposure can keep the mission alive.

questions.prompt: In Gideon's seminar, which test best separates coherent decentralization from disorder?
choices: Whether the system uses modern collaboration tools
Whether it stays harder to target while remaining clear enough to run internally
Whether nobody can identify any leader at all

explanation.gentle: Gideon keeps the chapter tied to architecture rather than to style.
explanation.direct: Keep the distinction sharp: resilience means attack gets harder without operations becoming blurry.
explanation.competitive: If the enemy loses the map but your team keeps it, the design is working.

questions.prompt: Cerys wants to reduce single-point risk on a client account. Which move best fits the chapter?
choices: Make the account lead handle every client interaction personally
Avoid documenting anything sensitive
Spread updates and records across the team while keeping internal ownership explicit

explanation.gentle: The move is to distribute exposure without erasing responsibility.
explanation.direct: Test the structure: redundancy helps only if people still know who owns the next action.
explanation.competitive: Break the shutdown point, not the command line.

questions.prompt: Halden is asked to become the lone public face of a sensitive neighborhood effort. When does refusing make strategic sense?
choices: Whenever visibility feels emotionally uncomfortable
When one public face would hand a hostile campaign too much leverage over the whole effort
Only when he plans to leave the effort soon anyway

explanation.gentle: The chapter allows lower visibility when it removes an unnecessary strike point.
explanation.direct: Separate caution from avoidance: the refusal is strategic when visibility would create a decisive target.
explanation.competitive: Skipping the stage is smart if the stage comes with a bullseye that could sink the mission.

questions.prompt: A student team says its work is decentralized, but no one can name who restores access after a system failure. What is the strongest diagnosis?
choices: The structure may be diffused, but it is not yet coherent enough to count as resilient
The team has already mastered the void strategy
The lack of ownership proves hierarchy is always weak

explanation.gentle: The chapter says denial of target is not enough if the system cannot recover clearly.
explanation.direct: Check responsibility first: resilience requires visible recovery ownership inside the team.
explanation.competitive: Fog is not strength. If no one can restore the system, the team is bluffing.

questions.prompt: Which judgment best captures the chapter's limit?
choices: Any diffuse structure is preferable to a visible leader
The strategy works only if outsiders never notice the group exists
The strategy is strong only while reduced target value does not come at the cost of mission control

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps asking whether the system remains able to act after it becomes harder to strike.
explanation.direct: Judge the trade carefully: lower exposure is valuable only while internal control stays intact.
explanation.competitive: Once mission control starts dissolving, the void is eating your side faster than the enemy is.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 26 differ from the alliance logic that follows in Chapter 27?
choices: Chapter 26 wins by earning public legitimacy while Chapter 27 wins by seeking obscurity
Chapter 26 denies a clean target, while Chapter 27 makes stronger actors carry part of your effort because it serves them
Chapter 26 and Chapter 27 both rely on the same mechanism of moral framing

explanation.gentle: The bridge turns from surviving attack through diffusion to gaining motion through aligned interests.
explanation.direct: Bridge the chapters cleanly: this one removes the strike point, the next one recruits outside power through incentive.
explanation.competitive: Here you spoil the hit. Next chapter you make bigger players push your campaign for their own reasons.
